title: TURN YOUR SERVICE INTO AN OFFER WITH CHATGPT
content:
"I do bookkeeping" tells someone what skill you use. It does not yet tell them what they can buy.

An offer makes the service concrete. "Monthly bookkeeping for small home-service businesses" is already more useful because it identifies a customer, a type of work, and an ongoing structure.

AN OFFER CREATES BOUNDARIES
"Virtual assistant services" can mean almost anything. "Weekly inbox and calendar management for solo consultants, including inbox triage, scheduling, and one weekly planning update" gives both sides a clearer starting scope.

PRICING STRUCTURE SHOULD MATCH THE WORK
Defined projects may fit project pricing. Repeated standardized work may fit packages or retainers. Variable work may sometimes fit hourly billing. Repeating measurable units can fit per-unit pricing.

This guide does not need the perfect market price. It needs to determine what the customer is buying so later pricing and selling decisions have something concrete to work with.

OFFER STATEMENT TEMPLATE
"I provide [defined service] for [specific customer] to help them [specific result/problem], delivered [how/often], with [major scope boundaries]."

Example:
"I provide monthly bookkeeping cleanup and reconciliation for small home-service businesses, with monthly financial reports and a defined document-submission process."

This is not marketing copy. It is a plain-language description of what the customer can actually buy.

AN OFFER MAKES THE SERVICE BUYABLE

A capability is not yet a clear offer. "I do bookkeeping" leaves the customer to guess what that means. A defined offer identifies the customer, the result or work, the scope, the delivery pattern, and the boundaries.

This guide can help you move from a broad capability to something concrete enough to price and investigate. It should not decide how you will advertise it, generate leads, write sales content, or close customers. Those questions belong to the separate selling system.

FROM SKILL TO OFFER: A CONCRETE EXAMPLE

Start with:

"I do bookkeeping."

A customer still has questions. What kind? For whom? How often? What is included? What result are they buying?

Narrow it:

"I provide monthly bookkeeping for small home-service businesses."

Better, but still incomplete.

Define the offer further:

"I provide recurring monthly bookkeeping for small home-service businesses that need their transactions categorized, accounts reconciled, and monthly financial reports kept current. The package covers the agreed accounts and monthly workflow, with cleanup, tax preparation, payroll, and other work quoted or referred separately when they are outside scope."

Now the customer can begin to understand what the purchase actually is.

This does not mean those exact tasks or boundaries are right for a real bookkeeper. The example demonstrates the transformation: broad skill becomes a defined customer, recurring problem, scope, delivery pattern, and boundary.

WHY BOUNDARIES MAKE AN OFFER STRONGER

Beginners sometimes worry that specifying what is not included will make an offer less attractive. In practice, an undefined service can create mismatched expectations and unpredictable work.

A clear boundary tells both sides what the agreed payment buys. Additional work can then be declined, separately priced, or handled through another appropriate arrangement.

This guide should leave you with something concrete enough to investigate and eventually price. It should stop before deciding how to attract or persuade customers. That is the next system.

WHEN THE OFFER IS SPECIFIC ENOUGH

You do not need a clever package name.

You need to be able to complete this sentence:

"I provide [defined result or service] for [specific kind of customer] through [clear scope or delivery structure], with [important boundaries] handled separately."

Then ask whether another person could reasonably understand what they are buying without a fifteen-minute explanation.

If yes, you have probably moved far enough for this product.

Pricing the real offer, validating demand, finding customers, presenting the offer, and making sales belong to the next stage of the business.

OFFER LANGUAGE DOES NOT OVERRIDE PROFESSIONAL RULES

Defining a clear scope is useful, but a scope statement cannot authorize work you are not qualified or permitted to perform.

If the service enters a regulated or professionally restricted area, verify the applicable requirements before finalizing what you promise customers.

HOW TO USE THIS
Use the prompt below to turn this branch into your version of the business. Answer the questions honestly, ask for clarification when you need it, and do not treat external facts as verified just because ChatGPT mentions them.

This guide defines the service the customer can buy. It stops before lead generation, marketing channels, content strategy, funnels, sales scripts, or closing. Those belong to HOW DO I SELL IT?

WHAT THIS INTERVIEW SHOULD PRODUCE

By the end, you should have a plain-language offer that identifies the customer, the service or result, the scope, the delivery structure, and important boundaries.

ChatGPT should help make the offer concrete without crossing into marketing strategy.

It should stop before lead generation, content plans, funnels, advertising, sales scripts, closing tactics, or other How Do I Sell It? work. The goal here is to define what you are selling. Finding buyers comes later.

COPY & PASTE INTO CHATGPT

During the interview:
- Ask one question at a time unless a small group of tightly related questions is genuinely easier to answer together.
- Use my answers before deciding what to ask next. Do not run through a generic questionnaire when an answer makes a question irrelevant.
- If I say "I don't know," help me identify what I need to decide or research. Do not silently invent an answer for me.
- Explain unfamiliar business terms in plain language when they first become relevant.
- Separate assumptions from facts that require outside verification.
- Do not turn this into a marketing or customer-acquisition plan unless the purpose of this specific interview requires it.
- When you have enough information, stop interviewing me and give me the requested conclusion, including the important unknowns and next research questions.
Ask me one question at a time unless a small group of closely related questions would be easier to answer together. If I say I don't know, help me identify what I would need to decide or research instead of inventing an answer for me.

Help me turn my service idea into a clear offer. Interview me about the specific customer, the problem or result, what work is included, what is excluded, deliverables, frequency or timeline, communication, boundaries, onboarding, capacity, and the pricing structure that fits the service.

Help me compare structures such as project pricing, packages, retainers, recurring fees, per-unit pricing, or hourly pricing where appropriate. Do not choose a price by inventing market data. Identify what I need to research.

Do not move into traffic, funnels, ads, content strategy, or outreach. I am defining what I sell, not how I will sell it.

End with a concise offer statement and scope.

NEXT → PDF 46 if clear; PDF 45 if time dependence is now the main concern.

While interviewing me, follow these rules:

Keep the offer narrow enough that a customer can understand what they are buying and the provider can understand what they must deliver.

Do not drift into promotion, audience growth, ads, funnels, social media strategy, or sales scripts. Those belong to the later HOW DO I SELL IT? system.

If pricing comes up, help choose a pricing STRUCTURE and identify inputs needed for a price. Do not invent a market price.

At the end, give me:
- Offer statement
- Customer
- Included work
- Excluded work
- Deliverables
- Delivery timing/frequency
- Communication boundaries
- Pricing structure
- Capacity constraint
- Facts still requiring research
